# Load necessary libraries
# install.packages(c("tidyverse", "janitor", "lubridate", "readxl", "here", "validate", "knitr"))
library(tidyverse)
library(readr)
library(janitor)
library(lubridate)
library(readxl)
library(here)
library(validate)
library(kableExtra)


# Import water quality data and metadata
# Specify col_types from the start to handle known formatting issues
yarra_wq <- read_excel(
  here("data/yarra_wq.xls"),
  col_types = c("numeric", "text", "text", "text", "numeric", 
                "text", "numeric", "text", "numeric", "text")
) %>%
  clean_names()

SW_Metadata <- read_csv(here("data/SW Metadata.csv"))%>% 
  clean_names()

# Inspect data structure
glimpse(yarra_wq)

The yarra_wq dataset includes columns like site_id (numeric), datetime (text), parameter (text), value (numeric), quality (text), and others. The datetime column is text due to a leading single quote in the raw data, which requires parsing.

Question 1 : Conduct an IDA

Data Screening for checking types of variables:

  • datetime: Convert data type from to due to a leading single quote in the raw data, which requires parsing.

  • site_id, value, parameter_id : These are numeric values, which is exactly what they should be.

  • name and parameter: These are text or character (chr) strings, which is appropriate for descriptive labels.

# Parse datetime column robustly
yarra_wq_process <- yarra_wq %>%
  mutate(
    datetime_text = str_trim(datetime, side = "both"),
    datetime = coalesce(
      excel_numeric_to_date(as.numeric(datetime_text)),
      ymd_hms(datetime_text, quiet = TRUE)
    )
  )

# Check missing values
missing_summary <- yarra_wq_process %>%
  summarise(
    missing_site_id = sum(is.na(site_id)),
    missing_datetime = sum(is.na(datetime)),
    missing_parameter = sum(is.na(parameter)),
    missing_value = sum(is.na(value))
  )

kable(missing_summary, 
      caption = "Summary of Missing Values After Datetime Parsing",
      booktabs = TRUE) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"), 
                full_width = FALSE)
Summary of Missing Values After Datetime Parsing
missing_site_id missing_datetime missing_parameter missing_value
0 0 0 0

The table shows the missing values in datetime are resolved after parsing datetime.

# Remove duplicates, keeping first occurrence
yarra_wq_process <- yarra_wq_process %>%
  distinct(site_id, datetime, parameter, .keep_all = TRUE)

# Remove unreasonable values as value must be positive
# pH range must be 0-14 
yarra_wq_clean <- yarra_wq_process %>%
  filter( value >= 0, 
          !(parameter == "pH" & (value < 0 | value > 14))
  ) %>%
  # Create the required date feature columns
  mutate(
    site_id = as.factor(site_id),
    date = as_date(datetime),
    year = year(datetime),
    month = month(datetime, label = TRUE),
    day = day(datetime),
    weekday = wday(datetime, label = TRUE),
    hour = hour(datetime)
  ) %>%
  select(
    site_id, name, date, year, month, day, weekday, hour,
    parameter, value, unit_of_measurement, quality, resolution
  )

# Inspect cleaned data
glimpse(yarra_wq_clean)

# Write the cleaned data to a new file as required
write_csv(yarra_wq_clean, here("data", "yarra_wq_clean.csv"))

To compare water quality between the 1990s and recent years, we identify sites and parameters with sufficient measurements in both periods (1990–1999 and 2015–present).

# Filter out the 1990s and recent years periods.
data_1990s <- yarra_wq_clean %>%
  filter(year >= 1990 & year < 2000) %>%
  count(site_id, name, parameter, name = "count_1990s")

data_recent <- yarra_wq_clean %>%
  filter(year >= 2015) %>%
  count(site_id, name, parameter, name = "count_recent")

sufficient_data <- inner_join(
  data_1990s, data_recent,
  by = c("site_id", "name", "parameter"))

kable(sufficient_data, 
      caption = 
        "Sites and Parameters with Sufficient Measurements in 1990s and Recent Years",
      booktabs = TRUE,
      col.names = c(
        "Site ID", "Site Name", "Parameter", "Count (1990s)", "Count (Recent)")) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"), 
                full_width = FALSE)

Table 1 shows that only site_id 229143 (“YARRA @ CHANDLER HWY”) has consistent measurements in both periods for parameters like Salinity, Turbidity, Water Temperature, and pH. Nitrogen and Phosphorus have limited recent data, making them less suitable for robust comparison.

Limitations

  • Single Site: Analysis is limited to site_id 229143, reducing spatial coverage.

  • Parameter Coverage: Nitrogen and Phosphorus have insufficient recent data, limiting the scope of water quality analysis.

  • Quality Filtering: Excluding non-“good” quality records reduces the dataset size, potentially affecting statistical power.

  • Duplicates: If duplicates were found, retaining only the first occurrence may discard valid repeated measurements.

The cleaned dataset (yarra_wq_clean.csv) is ready for further analysis, focusing on site_id 229143 and the parameters Salinity, Turbidity, Water Temperature, and pH.

Question 2: Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)

1. Numerical Summaries

# Filter for the specific site and the most viable parameters for comparison
# Create the period column for comparison
yarra_wq_compare <- yarra_wq_clean %>%
  filter(site_id == 229143,
         parameter %in% c("pH", "Salinity as EC@25", "Turbidity", "Water Temperature"))%>%
         mutate(period = case_when(
           year >= 1990 & year < 2000 ~ "1990s", 
           year >= 2010 ~ "Recent"
         )) %>%
  filter(!is.na(period)) 

# Calculate summary statistics
numerical_summary <- yarra_wq_compare %>%
  group_by(parameter, period) %>%
  summarise(
    count = n(),
    mean = round(mean(value, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    std_dev = round(sd(value, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    median = round(median(value, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    .groups = 'drop'
  ) %>%
  arrange(parameter, period)

kable(numerical_summary, 
      caption = "Summary Statistics for Water Quality Parameters at Site 229143",
      booktabs = TRUE,
      col.names = c(
        "Parameter", "Period", "Count", "Mean", "Standard Deviation", "Median")) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"), 
                full_width = FALSE)

The summary in Table 2 shows that the water quality at Chandler Highway has changed in complex ways, not just declined. Some indicators have worsened, while others have actually improved.

  • Salinity (EC@25): The average salinity (mean) is slightly higher and and as shown by the increase in the standard deviation, the values are much more variable in recent years. Even though the typical value (median) has not changed, this increased variability suggests a less stable environment.

  • Turbidity: Both of mean and median value have decreased. This is a positive sign, indicating the water is clearer in recent years than it was in the 1990s.

  • Water Temperature: The average water temperature (mean) has clearly increased. This is a negative sign for water quality because higher water temperatures reduce the amount of dissolved oxygen available for aquatic life, which supports the idea of a decline.

  • pH: The pH level is now more stable and closer to the neutral value of 7.0. The standard deviation dropped significantly, which points to a healthier and more stable water system.

Overall, we cannot say the water quality has simply declined. While the rising water temperature is a concern, other important measures like water clarity (lower turbidity) and pH stability have improved. The complaint from the Rakali organisation may only reflect one aspect of a more complicated situation.

2. Graphical Summaries

# Create side-by-side plots for each parameter
ggplot(yarra_wq_compare, aes(x = period, y = value, fill = period)) +
  geom_violin(alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, alpha = 0.5, size = 0.5) + 
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("1990s" = "skyblue", "Recent" = "salmon")) +
  facet_wrap(~ parameter, scales = "free_y", ncol = 2) +
  labs(
    title = "Water Quality Comparison: 1990s vs. Recent Years",
    subtitle = "At Chandler Highway Monitoring Site",
    x = "Period",
    y = "Measured Value") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + 
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 18, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5, 
                              margin = margin(b = 10)),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 14, hjust = 0.5, margin = margin(b = 15)),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold"),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 10),
    strip.text = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold"),
    panel.spacing = unit(1, "lines"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "none"
  )

The violin plots in Figure 1 reveal a fundamental shift in the river’s state between the 1990s and recent years:

  • Negative Indicators:

The Water Temperature distribution has unequivocally shifted to a warmer regime. Similarly, the wider shape of the Salinity violin for the recent period points to increased variability and instability.

  • Positive Indicators:

The most compelling evidence of improvement comes from Turbidity and pH. The recent Turbidity distribution is concentrated at much lower values, indicating a significant increase in water clarity. For pH, the recent distribution is remarkably narrow and tall, signifying a dramatic decrease in variance. This points to a more stable and resilient system with a stronger buffering capacity against acid or alkaline inputs.

Exploring Parameter Relationships

To add more depth, we can explore whether the relationships between parameters have changed over time.

# Reshape data to wide format for scatter plots
yarra_wq_wide <- yarra_wq_compare %>%
  mutate(parameter = case_when(
    parameter == "Salinity as EC@25" ~ "Salinity",
    parameter == "Water Temperature" ~ "Water_Temperature",
    TRUE ~ parameter
  )) %>%
  select(date, parameter, value, period) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = parameter,
    values_from = value,
    values_fn = mean
  ) %>%
  drop_na() 

# Plot 1: Turbidity vs Salinity
ggplot(yarra_wq_wide, aes(x = Turbidity, y = Salinity, color = period)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, linewidth = 1.2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("1990s" = "skyblue", "Recent" = "salmon")) +
  labs(
    title = "Relationship between Turbidity and Salinity",
    x = "Turbidity",
    y = "Salinity"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

The relationship between Turbidity and Salinity, shown in Figure 2, reveals a fundamental shift in the river’s response to runoff. In the 1990s, a weak negative correlation existed where higher turbidity was associated with lower salinity, suggesting a classic dilution effect from rainfall. However, in the recent period, this trend has reversed to a positive correlation. This change indicates that the impact of rainfall on water quality has evolved, possibly due to increased urbanization where runoff now carries a higher salt load into the river system.

# Plot 2: Water Temperature vs pH
ggplot(yarra_wq_wide, aes(x = Water_Temperature, y = pH, color = period)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, linewidth = 1.2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("1990s" = "skyblue", "Recent" = "salmon")) +
  labs(
    title = "Relationship between Water Temperature and pH",
    x = "Water Temperature",
    y = "pH"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

As illustrated in Figure 3, the relationship between water temperature and pH has fundamentally changed. In the 1990s, a clear positive correlation existed, indicating a reactive system where pH was sensitive to temperature changes. In the recent period, this relationship has disappeared, with the trend line becoming almost flat. This demonstrates that the river’s pH is now more stable and robust, and is no longer significantly influenced by temperature fluctuations, which suggests an improvement in chemical resilience.

Question 3 : Check your findings

1. Testing the Change in the Water Temperature-pH Relationship

Original Finding: The scatter plot reveals a significant shift in the relationship between water temperature and pH. In the 1990s, a positive correlation existed, suggesting a system where pH was sensitive to temperature changes. In the recent period, this correlation has vanished, with the trend line becoming flat, indicating a more stable and buffered system.

Null Hypothesis (\(H_0\)): There is no linear relationship between water temperature and pH within each period (slope = 0). Additionally, any observed difference in slopes between the 1990s and Recent periods is due to random variation, not a systematic change.

library(nullabor)
set.seed(123)

# Lineup Plot for Turbidity-Salinity
lineup(
    null_permute("pH"), 
    yarra_wq_wide,
    n = 20
  )%>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Water_Temperature, y = pH, color = period)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.2) + 
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, linewidth = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("1990s" = "skyblue", "Recent" = "salmon")) +
  facet_wrap(~ .sample, ncol = 5) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 16),
    panel.border = element_rect(colour = "grey80", fill = NA),
    legend.position = "none" 
  ) 
nullabor::pvisual(8, 10, 20)
     x simulated   binom
[1,] 8         0 1.6e-09

We can confidently reject the null hypothesis based on the lineup plot test that 8 out of 10 observers correctly identified the plot #20 as the most different from the null plots, which corresponds to a p-value of 1.6e-09 under the null hypothesis of random guessing.

While the relationship between water temperature and pH remains weak, the data provides evidence for: (1) a detectable linear association between water temperature and pH that differs from pure random variation, and (2) systematic differences in this relationship between the 1990s and recent periods.

The finding from our EDA is statistically significant: the relationship between water temperature and pH has fundamentally changed over the decades. The shift from a temperature-sensitive system in the 1990s to a stable, temperature-independent system in recent years is a real and meaningful feature of the data.

2. Testing the Change in Water Temperature

Original Finding: Our EDA showed a clear and significant increase in Water Temperature in recent years.

Null Hypothesis (\(H_0\)): The distribution of Water Temperature values is independent of the period(1990s vs. Recent). Any apparent difference between the two periods in our plot is simply due to random variation.

# Lineup Plot for Temperature
set.seed(456)

temp_data <- yarra_wq_compare %>%
  filter(parameter == "Water Temperature")

lineup(
  method = null_permute("period"), 
  true = temp_data, 
  n = 20
) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = period, y = value)) +
  geom_violin(fill = "gray70", color = "black") +
  facet_wrap(~ .sample, ncol = 5) +
  theme_void() + 
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 16),
    panel.border = element_rect(colour = "grey80", fill=NA))
nullabor::pvisual(6, 10, 20)
     x simulated   binom
[1,] 6         0 2.8e-06

We can reject the null hypothesis based on the results of the lineup test. When the plot was presented to 10 independent observers, 6 correctly identified plot #11 as the one most different from the null plots, which corresponds to a p-value of 2.8e-06 under the null hypothesis of random guessing.

This provides strong statistical evidence that the finding from our EDA is significant. The observed increase in water temperature is a real feature of the data, not a random artifact. We can therefore confidently conclude that the water at this location has become significantly warmer in recent years compared to the 1990s.

3. Testing the Change in pH Stability

Original Finding: Our EDA revealed that while the median pH changed only slightly, its variability decreased dramatically in recent years, suggesting the system has become significantly more stable.

Null Hypothesis (\(H_0\)): The distribution of pH values is independent of the period(1990s vs. Recent). Any apparent difference in the shape or spread of the violins is due to random chance.

# Lineup Plot for pH
set.seed(789)

pH_data <- yarra_wq_compare %>%
  filter(parameter == "pH")

lineup(
  method = null_permute("period"), 
  true = pH_data, 
  n = 20
) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = period, y = value)) +
  geom_violin(fill = "gray70", color = "black") +
  facet_wrap(~ .sample, ncol = 5) +
  theme_void() + 
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 16),
    panel.border = element_rect(colour = "grey80", fill=NA))
nullabor::pvisual(3, 10, 20)
     x simulated binom
[1,] 3     0.018 0.012

We can reject the null hypothesis based on the results of the lineup test. When the plot was presented to 10 independent observers, 3 correctly identified plot #13 as the one most different from the null plots, which corresponds to a p-value of 0.012 under the null hypothesis of random guessing.

Therefore, we can conclude that the finding from our EDA is supported: the pH of the river at this location has become significantly more stable in recent years. The visual test confirms that the observed decrease in variability is a real feature of the data.
